subsystems.name: Motor core
subsystems.role: converts electrical current into torque inside the smallest possible envelope.

subsystems.name: Gear reduction
subsystems.role: trades speed for torque so a small, fast motor can move a heavy limb.
parts: planetary gear stages, or a strain-wave (harmonic) cup

subsystems.name: Sensing
subsystems.role: tells the controller exactly where the joint is and how hard it is pushing.
parts: magnetic or optical encoders on motor and output

subsystems.name: Drive electronics
subsystems.role: converts DC bus power into the precise three-phase waveform the motor needs.

subsystems.name: Thermal and mechanical housing
subsystems.role: holds the air gap and gear mesh to tight tolerances while dumping heat.

subsystems.name: Control firmware
subsystems.role: makes the whole assembly behave like a compliant, responsive muscle.

buildSteps.title: Set the torque and thermal target
buildSteps.detail: Engineers choose a torque constant, gear ratio and duty cycle so the joint can hold a person-sized load without overheating. A low ratio keeps the joint backdrivable; a high ratio buys torque at the cost of transparency.

buildSteps.title: Design the magnetic circuit
buildSteps.detail: Stator slots, winding turns and magnet grade are laid out to maximise torque per amp while keeping iron losses and cogging low.

buildSteps.title: Wind and assemble the motor
buildSteps.detail: Copper wire is wound into the stator slots, magnets are glued into the rotor, and the rotor is balanced and fitted into the stator with a controlled air gap.

buildSteps.title: Cut and assemble the gearset
buildSteps.detail: Planetary gears are cut and ground, or a thin flexing strain-wave cup is machined; the reduction stage is then shimmed to near-zero backlash.

buildSteps.title: Fit bearings and output flange
buildSteps.detail: A cross-roller bearing carries the bending loads a limb experiences, so the gearbox itself never has to.

buildSteps.title: Integrate electronics and sensors
buildSteps.detail: The inverter board, encoders and temperature sensors are mounted inside or beside the housing, and control firmware is flashed and tuned.

buildSteps.title: Test and characterise
buildSteps.detail: The actuator is swept through its torque–speed range, its efficiency map is measured, and it is run hot to confirm the thermal limit.

buildSteps.title: Qualify for the robot
buildSteps.detail: Units are run through impact, dust and vibration tests before being built into a leg or arm.

prerequisites.why: neodymium-iron-boron magnets give the strongest field per kilogram, which is what makes a small motor powerful.
low-backlash planetary and strain-wave gearsets are what let a fast motor drive a slow, strong joint accurately.
field-oriented control at tens of kilohertz needs capable MOSFETs and microcontrollers at a price a robot can carry dozens of.
a joint cannot be controlled smoothly without knowing its angle to a fraction of a degree.
actuators are sealed inside limb shells, so heat must leave through potting, housings or oil rather than air.

pathway.milestone: quasi-direct-drive and geared actuator modules used in legged and humanoid robots
pathway.unlocks: machines that can walk, jump and recover balance with human-like dynamics.

pathway.milestone: joints that combine motor, gearbox, drive, sensing and cooling in one sealed, mass-produced unit
pathway.unlocks: cheaper, more reliable limbs and faster robot assembly.

pathway.milestone: higher bus voltages with silicon-carbide drives and integrated liquid cooling
pathway.unlocks: more torque from the same size, and sustained rather than burst performance.

pathway.milestone: alternative actuation such as electrohydrostatic or artificial-muscle drives
pathway.unlocks: lighter, softer limbs with torque density that motors and gears alone struggle to reach.
